Thank you for the positive comments.

Our method does not surpass the current SOTA method in the SLEEP dataset as GRAPHSENSOR is not specifically designed for classification of sleep stages or outperforming SOTA methods which are multi-channel based (inter-sensor representation learning). In this work, we provide a new idea that leverages intra-sensor dependencies for representation learning in time series sensory data. We have seen a number of works denoting inter-sensor dependencies as graphs, but our work is the first in intra-sensor, which is conceptually novel. We will change the title to “GRAPHSENSOR: A Graph Attention Network for Intra-sensor Representation Learning” if accepted to highlight our contribution.

content.title: Response to Reviewer vaNK
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments.

We notice you are concerned of our baseline selection and novelty (a little doubt though), we would like to clarify some misunderstandings:

(1)  “The paper misses some of the more recent baselines on sleep staging which surpasses the methods the paper compares against.”, “[1] and [2] surpasses DeepSleepNet by more than 4% while this method surpasses it by 3%.”, and “Other attention based methods perform as well as this for sleep staging.”

Based on a literature review of SOTA methods, we find most of them are developed from a multi-channel perspective. Specifically, in [1], the authors used all combinations of available EEG and EOG channels for each PSG, while [2] applied EEG+EOG+EMG to conduct their experiments. In this work, we present GRAPHSENSOR for modeling the internal relationships among signal segments generated by an individual sensor channel, which does not receive enough attention yet from the research community. As opposed to revealing a weakness in our work, we believe that "[1] and [2] surpass DeepSleepNet by more than 4%, whereas this method surpasses it by 3%" indicates a significant improvement in GRAPHSENSOR, as we use only one channel. We will include both [1] and [2] in our evaluation to further highlight our contribution if accepted.

(2) “It is not that important for sleep staging to be online so complexity might have a lower effect than on a real time use-case.” and “I can say it does not show any improvement over current  baselines. Moreover it does not have any additional motivation which might be important for healthcare like  explainability.”

GRAPHSENSOR is the first in intra-sensor study, by which we have discovered that internal relationships in the stream of sensor data has an important contribution in the classification of signals and cannot be discarded as shown in our ablation study (Q5-Q6, P7-8) and intra-sensor relationship visualization (Appendix D, P17-18). This study is fundamental to the online deployment of the proposed model, and we will evaluate the model performance on a real time use-case in the next study.
Please be noted that GRAPHSENSOR is not specifically designed for classification of sleep stage or out-performing SOTA multi-channel methods. In this work, we provide a new idea that leverages intra-sensor dependencies for representation learning in time series sensory data. We have seen a number of works denoting inter-sensor dependencies as graphs, but our work is the first in intra-sensor, which is conceptually novel. In experiments (Q1-Q2, P7-8), the presented graph attention network can also achieve state of the art results with significant model size reduction.

[1] Perslev, Mathias, et al. "U-Sleep: resilient high-frequency sleep staging." NPJ digital medicine 4.1 (2021): 1-12.

[2] Van Der Donckt, Jeroen, et al. "Do Not Sleep on Linear Models: Simple and Interpretable Techniques Outperform Deep Learning for Sleep Scoring." arXiv preprint arXiv:2207.07753 (2022).

content.title: Response to Reviewer jWJx
content.comment:
Thank you for  the comments. 

We notice you pointed out some weaknesses of our work, and we would like to clarify them below:

(1) “the novelty of the proposed methods is not much”

GRAPHSENSOR provides a new idea that leverages intra-sensor dependencies for representation learning in time series sensory data. We have seen a number of works denoting inter-sensor dependencies as graphs, but this work is the first in intra-sensor, which is conceptually novel. Our convolution-based multi-head attention also reduces the number of parameters as found out by other reviewers. Moreover, through our ablation study (Q3-Q6, P7-P8) and intra-sensor relationship visualization (Appendix D, P17-P18), we have shown that exploring internal relationships in the stream of sensor data can improve the classification accuracy especially for those subtle and confounding activities. This finding can lead to a new direction of extensive research into combined intra and inter-sensor relationship exploration, which can eventually help improve the multi-modal sensor fusion applications as highlighted at the end of the conclusion (page 9).

(2) “more background of the problem”

A full paragraph of the Introduction (the second paragraph of the Introduction) has been devoted to explaining the background of the problem. We highlight two key reasons why intra-sensor dependencies are crucial to recognizing human behavior and why we need to pay more attention to them. Furthermore, we analyze SOTA methods and identify research gaps that inspired us to design GRAPHSENSOR as a pioneer in intra-sensor studies (see the third paragraph of the Introduction).

(3) “more datasets and more evaluations would be necessary”

The Sleep-EDF-20 and WISDM datasets are significantly different, allowing the study of two important sensor data domains, i.e., bio sensors data and IMUs. Due to their wide application in various areas, such as health tracking，diabetes management and human activity recognition, we conduct our experiments using these two types of data. Additionally, we found that compared with other data types (such as audio signals), bio sensor signals and IMU signals change over time due to external and internal processes [1][2], which motivated us to investigate what processes were related to the activities we were interested in and what processes were not (noises).  Also, biosensor signals and IMU signals contain "rich temporal information"[1][2]. As this is a pioneer study in intra-sensor work, we believe it is sensible to begin our research from these two sources. In the evaluation, we propose six important research questions, and over 25 relevant experiments have been conducted to address these six research concerns. Moreover, the Appendix (page 17) contains a relationship visualization and discussion.

(4) “More deeper and broader description about related works other than Transformer and graph neural networks would be necessary”
Based on the architecture of GRAPHSENSOR (i.e., Feature Representation module and Relationship Learning module), we discuss the most related works from two important viewpoints, i.e., Feature Representation and Relationship Learning. We mainly discuss the Transformer and graph neural networks in the Relationship Learning part as these two methods are the SOTA to learn the signal relationships. Additionally, it is important to note that we discuss the Feature Representation methods (page 8-9), including various RNN and CNN-based methods, and most of these models mentioned in this subsection are also used as baselines to compare with the performance of GRAPHSENSOR, such as [3][4] (page 6).

(5) “Long history of feature learning of audio signals” and “WaveNet”

Our main research target is time-series sensor data, specially single channel serial data in this paper. The mentioned WaveNet is a deep generative model of raw audio waveforms that is developed to generate speech, which mimics any human voice and sounds more natural than the existing Text-to-Speech systems. Our research motivation is not quite the same as that of WaveNet. Furthermore, WaveNet's key module is the convolutional layer, which has various dilation factors that allow its receptive field to grow exponentially with depth and cover thousands of timesteps. We would like to draw your attention to one of our baseline algorithms, "AttnSleep" [Eldele et al., 2021, in page 6], which has a very similar architecture to WaveNet. The results of our experiment indicate that GRAPHSENSOR is capable of achieving the same performance with only one channel sensor data.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper proposed a framework called GRAPHSENSOR to capture the internal relationships in time-series data. In particular, the authors divided each sample into segments and learned the internal relationships among segments via graph attention networks. 

Strengths:
1. The paper is clearly written. The proposed model is also clearly described.
2. Using GNN to capture the internal relationships in the time-series data is new, which is clearly different from RNN/transformer for modeling temporal dependency. 
3. Shows great performance improvement in IMU sensor data .

Weaknesses:
1. Quite a number of time-series representation learning methods have been proposed recently, including TS-TCC, TS2vec, TNC, BTSF, etc. Discussions and comparisons with these methods are missing. In particular, the results of current baselines are quite poor on WISDM data. More recent and strong baselines are needed for WISDM data.
2. No performance improvement on sleep stage classification task. The authors are suggested to include 1-2 more tasks with single-channel data to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Alternatively, if the authors can work on intra- and inter-sensor relationships for multi-variate time series data, the method will be more promising and general. The contributions will also be further enhanced.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: There are critical concerns on the experimental evaluation part, i.e., more baselines (e.g., time-series representation learning methods) and more time-series datasets with single-channel are needed to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
